key_terms.meaning: The common normal at the point of contact of two teeth must always pass through the pitch point; then ω₁/ω₂ = O₂P/O₁P is constant
The point where the pitch circles touch and where the line of centres is cut by the common normal
m = d/T = p/π, in mm; d is pitch circle diameter in mm, T is number of teeth, p is circular pitch in mm
Angle between the common tangent to the pitch circles and the line of action; 20° is standard, 14.5° is old practice
Average number of tooth pairs in mesh = arc of contact ÷ circular pitch; must exceed 1 for smooth transfer of load
The tooth needs a tough interior to resist bending fatigue and a hard surface to resist pitting wear
A dimensionless tooth-shape factor, Y = π·y, that converts the tooth to an equivalent parabola; it depends only on the number of teeth
σ_b = W_t / (m·b·Y), where W_t is tangential load in N, b is face width in mm, m is module in mm, Y is the Lewis form factor
Extra tooth load from impact of mesh errors at speed, W_d = W_t + (21v(bC + W_t))/(21v + √(bC + W_t)), with v in m/s and C a deformation factor in N/mm²
Limiting surface load W_w = d·b·Q·K, where Q = 2T_g/(T_g + T_p) and K is the wear load factor in N/mm² from the material pair
Angle between a helical tooth and the shaft axis; it sets the axial thrust, the overlap and the virtual tooth count
Side force on a helical gear, W_a = W_t·tan ψ, which must be carried by a bearing and adds to shaft bending
For a bevel gear, T_v = T / cos δ, the tooth count of the equivalent spur gear on the back cone, with δ the pitch cone angle
R_m = R − b/2, where R is the cone distance in mm and b is the face width in mm; loads are taken at this section, not at the large end
λ = tan⁻¹(l/(π·d_w)), where l is the lead in mm and d_w the worm pitch diameter in mm; it decides efficiency and self-locking
Product of driving tooth numbers ÷ product of driven tooth numbers; the overall speed ratio of a gear train
Give every gear +x with the arm fixed, then add +y to all rows; the fixed gear's total is set to zero to find x and y
A single load that does the same damage as a load spectrum, found by Miner's rule: W_eq = [(Σ n_i·W_i^p)/Σ n_i]^(1/p), with p the life exponent
A log-scale plot of input speed on one side and spindle speeds on the other, with one line per gear pair; slope shows the ratio and crossing lines show overlaps
φ = (N_max/N_min)^(1/(z−1)) for z spindle speeds in geometric steps; one gear group multiplies speeds by φ^p

takeaways: A gear pair transmits a truly constant ratio only because the involute keeps the common normal fixed through the pitch point.
Gear material is a system: a tough core for bending fatigue and a hard surface for pitting resistance, chosen with heat treatment and cost together.
Lewis treats the tooth as a cantilever and sizes the module; Buckingham then adds the dynamic load of speed and the wear load of surface stress, and the larger of the two checks governs.
Helical teeth carry more load quietly because contact line is longer, but the axial thrust they create must be handed to the bearings and the shaft.
Bevel gear teeth are designed as spur teeth of a virtual gear on the back cone, using the mean cone distance for the load.
In a worm drive, sliding contact makes friction, wear and heat the size-setting factors, not bending strength.
Every gear train is solved pair by pair; an epicyclic train needs the extra step of adding the arm rotation to the relative rotations.
A gearbox is sized by an equivalent life load from the load spectrum, then checked for bearings, lubrication and heat.
A multi-speed gearbox is a product of gear groups, and the ray diagram shows at a glance whether the speed steps are geometric and whether groups overlap.
bank_note: Long answers are almost always a full design check in sequence: choose the material, size the tooth by Lewis or its helical, bevel or worm form, then check the same tooth for dynamic load and wear (or friction and heat for a worm), and state which check governed.

bank.q: State the law of gearing. With a neat sketch of two involute teeth in contact, show that the common normal at the point of contact always cuts the line of centres at the pitch point, and hence that the angular velocity ratio stays constant throughout the mesh.
outline: Condition: common normal must pass through the pitch point P for constant ratio
Similar triangles O₁PN and O₂PM give ω₁/ω₂ = O₁P/O₂P
Involute property: the normal to an involute is tangent to its base circle, so the line of action is fixed in space
Therefore the normal always passes through P; ratio constant at every instant
Contrast with non-involute profiles where the normal shifts and the ratio fluctuates

bank.q: Define module, circular pitch, diametral pitch, pressure angle, addendum, dedendum, backlash and contact ratio for a spur gear pair. Give the relations between module, circular pitch and number of teeth, and state standard pressure angles used in practice.
outline: m = d/T = p/π, with units mm
Standard modules from preferred series; pressure angle usually 20°
Addendum = m, dedendum = 1.25 m in standard full-depth teeth
Backlash is the clearance between the trailing flanks
Contact ratio = arc of contact ÷ circular pitch; must be greater than 1

bank.q: A gear material must supply core strength, surface hardness and machinability at acceptable cost. Discuss how through-hardened alloy steel, case-carburised steel and cast iron meet these three needs, and explain when a hardened rim is used instead of a solid hardened gear.
outline: Core strength resists root bending fatigue; hardness resists pitting
Through-hardened steels: uniform hardness, simple, limited surface hardness
Case-carburised steels: hard case on tough core, best for high load and shock
Cast iron and bronze: cheap, quiet, low load, poor for high stress
Hardened rim on a soft hub: keeps toughness in the hub, saves cost, only for large gears

bank.q: Explain why a helical gear pair carries more load and runs quieter than a spur pair of the same size and material. Define helix angle, normal module and transverse module, and show how the axial thrust on the shaft is calculated.
outline: Oblique tooth gives gradual engagement; no sudden full-face impact
Longer total contact line and overlap greater than 1
m_n = m_t·cos ψ, and the virtual tooth count T/cos³ψ for strength
W_a = W_t·tan ψ
Thrust needs an angular-contact or taper roller bearing, or a double-helical arrangement to cancel it

bank.q: A motor delivers 7.5 kW at 1440 rpm to a spur gear pair with a speed ratio of 4 and a 20° pressure angle. Select a suitable steel and heat treatment, size the pinion module and face width by the Lewis equation with a velocity factor, then check the same tooth for Buckingham dynamic load and wear load. State clearly which check controls the design.
outline: Pitch line velocity and tangential load W_t = P/v, with power in W and v in m/s
Material allowable bending stress with the correct factor of safety
Table of Lewis form factor Y against tooth number; pick minimum teeth above undercut limit
Standard module selected from the preferred series; face width b = 10 m or as restricted
Dynamic load from Buckingham with the deformation factor C for the material pair
Wear load W_w = d·b·Q·K and comparison with the design load
Comparison of checks and conclusion on which governs

bank.q: Design a helical gear pair to transmit 15 kW at 1000 rpm of the pinion with a ratio of 3.5 and a helix angle of 20°. Use the modified Lewis equation with the virtual number of teeth and a helix factor, check the tooth for dynamic load, and compute the axial thrust for the bearing selection.
outline: Transverse and normal module relation; virtual tooth count T/cos³ψ
Modified Lewis with helix factor to reduce the allowable stress
Face width in terms of module; overlap ratio
Dynamic load check with pitch line velocity
W_a = W_t·tan ψ and the bearing type it forces
Effect of choosing a larger helix angle on load sharing versus thrust

bank.q: Design a straight bevel gear pair for a right-angle drive transmitting 4 kW at 900 rpm of the pinion, ratio 2.5, with shafts at 90°. Use the virtual spur gear on the back cone with the mean cone distance, apply Lewis for bending, and check wear on the same tooth.
outline: Pitch cone angles from the ratio: tan δ₁ = T₁/T₂
Cone distance R and face width b ≤ R/3
Virtual teeth T_v = T/cos δ and the corresponding Lewis form factor
Load taken at mean radius, i.e. using R_m = R − b/2
Tangential load from torque at mean radius, then bending check
Wear check with the appropriate Q for bevel teeth
Axial and radial components on the shaft for bearing choice

bank.q: A single-start worm rotating at 1440 rpm drives a 40-tooth worm wheel. The worm pitch diameter is 50 mm and the coefficient of friction is 0.05. Compute the lead angle, sliding velocity, efficiency and power lost as heat, and decide whether natural cooling of the gearbox casing is sufficient.
outline: Lead l = π·m·starts, and λ = tan⁻¹(l/π d_w)
Sliding velocity from the worm surface speed and lead angle
Efficiency η = tan λ (1 − μ tan λ) / (tan λ + μ) or the equivalent form
Heat generated = input power × (1 − η)
Heat dissipated from casing area and temperature rise above ambient
Conclusion on fins, fan or oil cooler

bank.q: A planetary gear train has a sun with 24 teeth, three planets with 18 teeth each and a fixed annulus. The sun runs at 600 rpm. Using the tabular method, find the arm speed and the planet speed, and state the train value.
outline: Check the geometry: annulus teeth = sun + 2 × planet
Rows: arm fixed, sun +x, each planet −x·T_s/T_p, annulus −x·T_s/T_a
Second row: add +y to every element to represent the arm rotation
Fixed annulus gives y in terms of x; solve for y
Arm speed = y, planet speed = y − x·T_s/T_p
Train value and direction of rotation of the arm

bank.q: A machine tool spindle needs six speeds from 100 rpm to 1000 rpm in geometric progression. Choose the progression ratio, decide the number of gear groups and their order, sketch the ray diagram, and explain how the tooth numbers of each pair are fixed.
outline: φ = (1000/100)^(1/5) and rounding to a standard value
Actual speeds and the small deviation from nominal
Product of group sizes equals the number of speeds; a two-shaft group is cheapest
Group order: more reduction earlier, smaller steps later
Ray diagram on log scale; slope of each ray equals the ratio of that pair
Overlaps and how they reduce the number of shafts
Tooth numbers from the ratios with a common module and a minimum tooth limit

bank.q: Bending fatigue at the root and pitting of the flank are the two competing limits on a spur gear. Compare them in terms of where the stress acts, what material property resists each, and how load, speed and surface hardness shift which one governs the design.
outline: Root bending: tensile stress on the fillet, resisted by core strength
Pitting: repeated Hertzian contact stress, resisted by surface hardness
Higher speed raises the dynamic load and worsens both, pitting more
Case hardening moves the limit to bending; through-hardening leaves pitting critical at high load
Design response: change module (bending) versus change hardness or face width (wear)
Practical conclusion on which check to tighten

bank.q: A crane duty gearbox sees a repeating load spectrum over its shift: light loads for most of the time and a few heavy lifts. Explain how the spectrum is converted into an equivalent load using Miner's rule, how the life in hours follows from the speed, and what changes if the heavy lifts become more frequent.
outline: S-N curve and the inverse-power life relation W^p·N = constant
Damage fraction per load level and the sum set equal to one
Equivalent load formula with the exponent p depending on the material and heat treatment
Life in revolutions then in hours at the operating speed
Sensitivity: more heavy lifts cut life sharply because of the exponent
Design response: increase module or hardness, or accept a shorter replacement interval

bank.q: A conveyor needs a 20:1 reduction in two stages. Discuss how you would split the ratio between the two stages, choose material and heat treatment for each stage, check the bearings and the heat, and use a ray diagram or speed chart to confirm the output speeds of a two-speed version.
outline: Ratio split so that the two stages have comparable size; larger reduction in the slower stage is common
Material choice: case-hardened pinion with through-hardened wheel, or both case-hardened
Load per stage from torque, with efficiency losses carried forward
Bearing selection from the radial and axial loads, including helical thrust if used
Heat balance by casing area and lubrication method
Speed chart to confirm all output speeds; reason for choosing helical for quietness

bank.q: Compare an epicyclic gear train with a sliding gear train for the spindle drive of a machine tool. Cover the speeds achievable, the number of gear pairs needed, compactness, efficiency and the difficulty of manufacture, and state which you would choose for a given speed range.
outline: Epicyclic: high reduction in a small space by combining sun, planet and annulus
Sliding gear train: geometric speed steps, simple kinematics, easy servicing
Number of pairs versus compactness comparison
Efficiency: epicyclic loses in planet bearings, sliding gears lose in mesh only
Manufacturing and noise differences
Recommendation tied to the required speed range and duty

glossary.def: A toothed wheel that transmits motion and torque to another toothed wheel by successive contact of teeth.
The smaller gear of a meshing pair, usually the driver.
The theoretical circle on which the gear ratio is calculated and on which the pitch point lies.
The pitch circle diameter in mm divided by the number of teeth; the basic size unit of gear teeth.
Arc length on the pitch circle between corresponding points of adjacent teeth, equal to π times the module.
The angle between the line of action and the common tangent to the pitch circles, usually 20°.
Radial height of a tooth above the pitch circle, equal to one module in standard teeth.
Radial depth of a tooth below the pitch circle, equal to 1.25 module in standard full-depth teeth.
The small clearance between the non-driving flanks of meshing teeth, allowing lubrication and thermal growth.
The curve traced by a point on a taut string unwound from a base circle; its normal is always tangent to the base circle.
The average number of tooth pairs in contact, equal to the arc of contact divided by the circular pitch.
Removal of material at the tooth root by the cutter when the tooth count is too low, weakening the tooth.
A factor depending on tooth number that gives the strength of the parabolic equivalent tooth.
The additional tooth load caused by impact and mesh errors at running speed.
The limiting tangential load set by surface contact stress, beyond which pitting starts.
Fatigue failure of the tooth surface appearing as small craters on the flank.
The angle a helical tooth makes with the shaft axis.
The tooth count of the equivalent spur gear used in strength formulas for helical and bevel gears.
The slant length from the apex to the large end of a bevel gear pitch cone.
The angle of the worm thread helix with the plane of rotation, controlling efficiency and self-locking.
The ratio of the product of driving teeth to the product of driven teeth for a whole train.
A train in which one or more gears move around a central axis while carried by a rotating arm.
A log-scale speed chart in which each gear pair appears as a straight ray, used to design multi-speed gearboxes.
The constant factor between consecutive spindle speeds in a geometric speed series.
A single steady load that causes the same fatigue damage as a varying load history over the same number of cycles.
